bmo-bmo1-2023-01.title: Bound k in the middle case
bmo-bmo1-2023-01.body:
The cases $n<200$ and $n\ge300$ are as in the first solution. For $n=199+x$ with $1\le x\le100$ we need
$$k=\frac{199+x}{11+x}=1+\frac{188}{11+x}$$
to be an integer. As $x$ runs from $1$ to $100$, $1+\frac{188}{11+x}$ decreases from $1+\frac{188}{12}\approx16.7$ to $1+\frac{188}{111}\approx2.7$, so $3\le k\le16$. Testing $k=3,\dots,16$, i.e. $11+x=\frac{188}{k-1}$, an integer only for $k-1\in\{2,4\}$ (divisors of $188$ in range): $k=3$ gives $x=83$, $n=282$; $k=5$ gives $x=36$, $n=235$.

Together with the multiples of $11$ in $[110,198]$ and of $111$ in $[333,999]$: $18$ values in all. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2023-02.title: Even terms from a₆ on are squares, odd ones are not
bmo-bmo1-2023-02.body:
**No two positive squares differ by 4.** If $y^2-x^2=(y-x)(y+x)=4$ with $y>x\ge0$, the factors have the same parity, so both equal $2$ and $x=0$.

**From $a_5$ on.** For $n\ge2$ we have $a_{2n}=a_{2n-1}+4$, so
$$a_{2n+2}=a_{2n+1}+4=a_{2n}a_{2n-1}+4=(a_{2n-1}+4)a_{2n-1}+4=(a_{2n-1}+2)^2 .$$
So $a_6,a_8,\dots,a_{2022}$ are all squares ($1009$ terms), while each $a_{2n+1}$ ($n\ge2$) is a positive integer $4$ less than the square $a_{2n+2}$, hence not a square. So $a_5,\dots,a_{2022}$ contain exactly $1009$ squares.

**The first four terms** are $a,\ b,\ ab,\ ab+4$. The last two differ by $4$, so at most one of them is a square; hence at most $3$ of the first four are squares.

So $m\le3+1009=1012$. If $a$ and $b$ are both squares then $ab$ is a square too, and $m=1012$; e.g. $a=b=1$ gives $1,1,1,5,5,9,45,49,\dots$.

**Answer: 1012.** ∎

bmo-bmo1-2023-03.title: Reflect A in the bisectors
bmo-bmo1-2023-03.body:
**$F$ is the midpoint of a segment from $A$ to line $BC$.** Line $CF$ bisects the angle $ACD$ (the exterior angle at $C$). Reflect $A$ in line $CF$ to get $F'$. Reflection in the bisector swaps the two arms of the angle, so $F'$ lies on ray $CD$, hence on line $BC$. Since $AF\perp CF$, the reflection of $A$ lies on line $AF$, and $F$ (the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $CF$) is the midpoint of $AF'$.

(Equivalently: let $AF$ meet $BC$ at $F'$; triangles $AFC$ and $F'FC$ are congruent by ASA — common side $CF$, right angles at $F$, equal angles at $C$ — so $AF=FF'$.)

**$G$ likewise.** $BG$ bisects angle $ABC$; reflecting $A$ in line $BG$ gives a point $G'$ on ray $BC$, and since $AG\perp BG$, $G$ is the midpoint of $AG'$.

**Conclusion.** The homothety with centre $A$ and ratio $\frac12$ maps $B\mapsto C_1$, $C\mapsto B_1$, $F'\mapsto F$, $G'\mapsto G$. The four points $B,C,F',G'$ lie on line $BC$, so their images $C_1,B_1,F,G$ lie on one line (the image of line $BC$, which is the midline $B_1C_1$). ∎

bmo-bmo1-2023-03.title: Circles on AB and AC as diameters
bmo-bmo1-2023-03.body:
Since $B_1,C_1$ are midpoints, $B_1C_1\parallel BC$; it is the unique line through $C_1$ (or through $B_1$) parallel to $BC$.

**$G$ lies on it.** $\angle AGB=90^\circ$, so $G$ lies on the circle with diameter $AB$, whose centre is $C_1$. Thus $C_1G=C_1B$ and $\angle C_1GB=\angle C_1BG=\angle GBA=\angle GBC$. The points $C_1$ (on side $BA$) and $C$ lie on opposite sides of the bisector $BG$, so these are alternate angles and $C_1G\parallel BC$. Hence $G$ is on the line through $C_1$ parallel to $BC$, i.e. on $B_1C_1$.

**$F$ lies on it.** $\angle AFC=90^\circ$, so $F$ is on the circle with diameter $AC$, centre $B_1$. Thus $B_1F=B_1C$ and $\angle B_1FC=\angle B_1CF=\angle ACF=\angle FCD$. Here $B_1$ (on side $CA$) and $D$ lie on opposite sides of line $CF$, so again these are alternate angles and $B_1F\parallel CD$, i.e. $B_1F\parallel BC$. So $F$ is on line $B_1C_1$ as well. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2023-04.title: Dominoes for Katy, a chessboard for Alex
bmo-bmo1-2023-04.body:
**Katy can always get at least 32.** Before the game she splits the board into $32$ dominoes ($1\times2$ rectangles). On each turn she fills a domino that is still completely empty.

This is always possible on her first $16$ turns. Each of Alex's moves spoils at most one domino, and each of Katy's moves uses up exactly one. Before Katy's $j$-th turn, Alex has made $j$ moves and she has made $j-1$, so at least $32-j-(j-1)=33-2j\ge1$ dominoes are still empty when $j\le16$. Alex can also always move before then, because at most $3(j-1)\le45<64$ cells are filled before his $j$-th move. So Katy makes at least $16$ moves and scores at least $32$.

**Alex can hold Katy to 32.** Colour the board like a chessboard: $32$ black and $32$ white cells. Alex always writes his A on an empty black cell while one exists. Any two cells sharing an edge have different colours, so each of Katy's moves also uses exactly one black cell.

As long as Alex has played on black, each full round (Alex, then Katy) uses two black cells. Before Katy's $j$-th move, $2j-1$ black cells are used, and this is at most $32$, so $j\le16$. If at some turn of Alex no black cell is empty, then Katy can never move again, since every move of hers needs a black cell. Either way Katy makes at most $16$ moves, i.e. writes at most $32$ Ks.

**Answer: 32.** ∎

bmo-bmo1-2023-04.title: Another strategy for Katy: 2×2 squares
bmo-bmo1-2023-04.body:
The upper bound $32$ is the chessboard argument from the first solution. Here is a different way for Katy to guarantee $32$.

Split the board into sixteen $2\times2$ squares; call a square *fresh* if all four of its cells are empty. Katy's rule:
- If Alex has just written in a fresh square, three cells of it remain empty, forming an L-shape, which contains two cells sharing an edge; Katy fills those two.
- Otherwise she fills two adjacent cells of some fresh square.

**Counting fresh squares.** In each round (Alex's move, then Katy's) at most one square stops being fresh: in the first case both moves are in the same square; in the second case Alex's move did not touch a fresh square and Katy uses one. So at the start of round $j$ at least $16-(j-1)$ squares are fresh, and in round $j\le16$ Katy can always follow her rule (the first case is always possible, and in the second case at least $17-j\ge1$ fresh squares remain). Alex can also always move in these rounds, since fewer than $64$ cells are filled.

So Katy makes at least $16$ moves, scoring at least $32$. Combined with Alex's chessboard strategy, the answer is **32**. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2023-05.title: Recurrence for n = pᵐq
bmo-bmo1-2023-05.body:
**Recurrence.** For $n>1$, classify the lists by their second-to-last term $d$: it is a proper divisor of $n$, and the lists ending $\dots,d,n$ correspond to the $f(d)$ lists ending in $d$. So
$$f(n)=\sum_{d\mid n,\ d<n}f(d). \tag{$\dagger$}$$

**Prime powers.** For a prime $p$ and $m\ge1$: $f(p^m)=2^{m-1}$. By strong induction: $f(p)=f(1)=1$, and
$$f(p^{k+1})=f(1)+\sum_{j=1}^{k}f(p^j)=1+(1+2+\dots+2^{k-1})=2^k .$$

**Numbers $p^mq$.** Let $q\ne p$ be another prime and $g(m)=f(p^mq)$, so $g(0)=f(q)=1$. The proper divisors of $p^{k+1}q$ are $p^0,\dots,p^{k+1}$ and $p^0q,\dots,p^kq$, while those of $p^kq$ are $p^0,\dots,p^k$ and $p^0q,\dots,p^{k-1}q$. Applying $(\dagger)$ to both,
$$g(k+1)=\Bigl[\textstyle\sum_{j\le k}f(p^j)+\sum_{j\le k-1}f(p^jq)\Bigr]+f(p^{k+1})+f(p^kq)=g(k)+2^k+g(k)=2g(k)+2^k .$$
By induction $g(m)=(m+2)2^{m-1}$: it holds for $m=0$ ($2\cdot\frac12=1$), and $2(m+2)2^{m-1}+2^m=(m+3)2^m$. (Check: $f(6)=g(1)=3$.)

**Choosing $n$.**
- $N=1$: any $n$ works.
- $N=2$: $f(4)=f(2^2)=2$.
- $N\ge3$: take $n=2^{N-2}\cdot3$; then $f(n)=g(N-2)=N\cdot2^{N-3}$, a multiple of $N$.

∎

bmo-bmo1-2023-05.title: Count ordered factorisations directly
bmo-bmo1-2023-05.body:
A valid list $1=a_0<a_1<\dots<a_k=n$ corresponds to the **ordered factorisation** $n=d_1d_2\cdots d_k$ with $d_i=a_i/a_{i-1}\ge2$, and conversely. So $f(n)$ is the number of ways to write $n$ as an ordered product of factors $\ge2$.

For $n=p^mq$ ($p\ne q$ primes, $m\ge1$), write the prime factors in a row, $p\cdots p\,q\,p\cdots p$, choose where $q$ goes and which gaps become "commas" (factor boundaries). To count each factorisation once, require that $q$ is either the last symbol or is immediately followed by a comma (within each factor, put $q$ last).
- $q$ last: the $m$ gaps between consecutive symbols are free: $2^m$ ways.
- $q$ in one of the $m$ positions followed by a $p$: the gap after $q$ must be a comma, the other $m-1$ gaps are free: $m\cdot2^{m-1}$ ways.

So $f(p^mq)=2^m+m2^{m-1}=(m+2)2^{m-1}$, and we conclude as in the first solution with $n=2^{N-2}\cdot3$ for $N\ge3$, $n=4$ for $N=2$. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2023-06.title: Rhombi and a chord parallel to l
bmo-bmo1-2023-06.body:
Let $O$ be the centre of $\Gamma$ and let the frog visit $a_0,a_1,a_2,\dots$, with $a_{\text{even}}\in\Gamma$ and $a_{\text{odd}}\in l$. Suppose, for contradiction, that $a_0,a_1,\dots,a_8$ are all different. We use vectors.

**Step 1: $a_1=a_0+a_2-O$.** The points at distance $1$ from both $a_0$ and $a_2$ (with $a_0\neq a_2$) lie on the perpendicular bisector of $a_0a_2$ and are symmetric about the midpoint of $a_0a_2$; there are at most two of them, namely $O$ and $O'=a_0+a_2-O$ (indeed $|O'-a_0|=|a_2-O|=1$ and $|O'-a_2|=|a_0-O|=1$). The point $a_1$ is one of them, and $a_1\neq O$ because $a_1\in l$ while $O\notin l$. So $a_1=a_0+a_2-O$, i.e.
$$a_1-a_0=a_2-O .$$
(Geometrically, $Oa_0a_1a_2$ is a rhombus.)

**Step 2.** In the same way, from $a_2,a_4\in\Gamma$ and $a_3\in l$ at distance $1$ from both, $a_3=a_2+a_4-O$, i.e. $a_3-a_4=a_2-O$.

**Step 3: $a_0a_4\parallel l$.** Combining, $a_1-a_0=a_3-a_4$, so
$$a_0-a_4=a_1-a_3 .$$
Since $a_1\ne a_3$ both lie on $l$, the vector $a_1-a_3$ is a nonzero vector along $l$. So the chord $a_0a_4$ of $\Gamma$ is parallel to $l$.

**Step 4.** Applying Steps 1–3 to $a_4,a_5,\dots,a_8$ shows the chord $a_4a_8$ is also parallel to $l$. But the line through $a_4$ parallel to $l$ meets $\Gamma$ in at most one point other than $a_4$, so $a_8=a_0$ — contradicting our assumption.

Hence among $a_0,\dots,a_8$ some point occurs twice: the frog returns to a point it has visited before within at most $8$ jumps. ∎

*Remark.* Step 3 can also be seen as a translation: the vector $\overrightarrow{a_0a_1}=\overrightarrow{Oa_2}=\overrightarrow{a_4a_3}$ carries triangle $a_0Oa_4$ onto triangle $a_1a_2a_3$, so $a_0a_4\parallel a_1a_3=l$.
